romanization_guidance: Sindhi's Perso-Arabic-based script includes implosive consonants and vowel distinctions that ordinary ASCII cannot represent precisely; choose the most common reader-friendly rendering and flag genuine vowel/consonant ambiguity via translation_note rather than presenting one romanization as definitively precise.
Use a widely-recognized conventional spelling for well-known names/places (e.g. a widely known poet or place name) when one already exists in common English usage.
Keep every repeated occurrence of the same source term romanized identically within one poem.
Do not use scholarly Perso-Arabic transliteration conventions (e.g. ayin/hamza marks, macrons) -- ASCII letters, spaces, apostrophes, and hyphens only, per the shared romanization policy.
linguistic_guidance: Sindhi vocabulary draws on Sufi-devotional, Persianate, Islamic, and Hindu-Sindhi registers; a term's origin in one of these traditions does not by itself indicate this poem's cultural specificity -- assess its actual role in this text.
Sindhi poetry has a strong oral/sung performance tradition (including the Sur/raga-associated forms); do not assume a specific performance context beyond what the text itself supports.
cultural_boundary_rules: A culturally specific Sindhi annotation requires a defensible link to a named tradition, practice, or symbol that the poem's own text actually evidences -- do not add one merely because the poem is in Sindhi.

Do not infer Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai or his Sur poetry, Sufi shrine imagery, Ajrak (block-print textile), the Sindhi topi (cap), desert landscapes, Indus-river imagery, or specific folk instruments unless the poem's own words name or unambiguously depict that specific content -- these are common outside shorthands for 'Sindhi culture' and must not be assumed as a default backdrop.

Words for love, soul, remembrance, journey, desert, river, and longing are not automatically Sindhi-specific cultural cues -- this vocabulary is shared across Sufi and South Asian devotional poetic traditions broadly; treat it as culturally specific only when the poem's own text gives it a specific, named, or clearly bounded Sindhi role.

Do not conflate Sufi-devotional and Hindu-Sindhi devotional registers (e.g. Jhulelal/Darya Shah veneration) -- both are genuine, distinct Sindhi traditions; annotate strictly by which the poem's own text actually evidences, and preserve ambiguity rather than defaulting to one when the text does not clearly indicate which.
literary_context_cautions: Sindhi literary tradition includes multiple distinct strands (classical Sur poetry, Sufi devotional verse, Hindu-Sindhi devotional verse, partition/displacement-era literature, contemporary verse) -- do not assume a poem belongs to a specific one without textual evidence.
Do not assume every Sindhi poem engages with partition or displacement; annotate only what the poem's own text supports.
translation_cautions: Watch for a named devotional practice (e.g. a specific Sufi practice) being translated with a generic English equivalent (e.g. 'prayer' or 'meditation') that loses its specific identity -- note this as translation loss.
Watch for Sufi-devotional vocabulary being flattened to generic mysticism vocabulary in translation, losing the tradition-specific register.
figurative_language_cautions: Sufi-register vocabulary (the beloved, wine, union, the journey) may be genuinely ambiguous between secular-romantic and devotional-mystic readings; resolve this only from the poem's own textual evidence, and use the explicit-uncertainty mechanism when it is genuinely unresolvable.
visual_representation_cautions: When a cultural or figurative element is genuinely visualizable, offer multiple acceptable_visual_variants rather than a single fixed scene, and do not default to shrine, desert, or Ajrak-textile imagery unless the text specifically supports it.

negative_confusions for a Sindhi entity should name a plausible, specific incorrect substitution -- for example, distinguishing a specific named devotional practice from generic prayer/meditation imagery, or distinguishing Sufi figures from an unrelated-religion generic holy-man stereotype -- not a generic stereotype disconnected from the poem's own evidence.
stereotype_avoidance_rules: Do not adopt a performative 'immersed in Sur poetry and Sufi tradition' framing when annotating -- annotate only what this specific poem's text supports.
Do not apply a numeric quota (e.g. 'expect N cultural entities') to this poem -- a Sindhi poem with zero or few text-supported cultural entities is a valid, expected outcome.
ambiguity_handling_rules: When a devotional term could plausibly belong to either the Sufi or Hindu-Sindhi register, or to either a secular-romantic or devotional-mystic reading, and the poem's own text does not disambiguate, prefer the more conservative reading and use the explicit-uncertainty mechanism rather than asserting one interpretation as fact.
prohibited_assumptions: Do not assume the speaker's religion (Sufi Muslim, Hindu Sindhi, or secular) beyond what the text states.
Do not assume a specific historical period (e.g. pre-partition, partition-era, contemporary) unless the text itself places the poem there.
Do not assume gender beyond what the text states.
